promptText: What does 'time-to-first-token' (TTFT) measure in an LLM request?
options: The time for the model to read and process the entire input prompt before producing the first output token
The total time from request sent to the full response being received
The time it takes the client to render the first character on screen
The average time per output token during decoding
explanation: TTFT is the prefill-phase latency: the time to process the full input prompt before any output token is produced. It scales roughly with input length and is distinct from decode time.

promptText: Why does streaming a response improve user experience even though it does not reduce total generation time?
options: It reduces the number of output tokens the model must generate
It lets the user see the first tokens after time-to-first-token instead of waiting for time-to-last-token, improving perceived latency only
It compresses the model's output using a smaller draft model
It caches the response so future identical requests are instant
explanation: Streaming changes perceived latency, not total compute: the model still generates every token, but the user sees output starting at TTFT rather than waiting for the full TTLT.

promptText: For a typical single-turn chat request, which phase usually accounts for 70-95% of total latency?
options: The Advisor chain's pre-call memory and RAG lookups
Prompt assembly and response serialization inside the Spring application
The prefill and decode phases running inside the model provider
Auth and rate-limiting checks at the gateway
explanation: Walking the request lifecycle shows that prefill and decode, both entirely inside the provider, dominate total latency for most requests -- everything the application controls is usually a small minority of the time budget.

promptText: Why is 'ask for a shorter answer' typically a stronger cost lever than 'send a shorter prompt'?
options: Output tokens are usually priced several times higher than input tokens because decode is the expensive, sequential phase
Input tokens are always billed at a flat rate regardless of length
Shorter prompts increase the risk of hallucination, so providers charge a premium
Output length has no effect on billed cost, only on latency
explanation: Because decode is sequential and expensive, providers typically price output tokens higher than input tokens, so trimming output length saves more money than trimming an equivalent number of input tokens.

promptText: What is the main requirement for a request to benefit from provider-side prompt/context caching?
options: The temperature must be set to exactly 1.0
The static, reusable part of the prompt must be byte-identical and positioned consistently (typically first) across calls
The request must use function calling
The prompt must be shorter than 100 tokens total
explanation: Provider-side prefix caching recognizes a byte-identical, stably-positioned prefix across calls; placing static content first and dynamic content last is what makes a prompt eligible for this discount.

promptText: What does the `maxTokens` parameter actually control?
options: The maximum number of input tokens the model will accept
The number of retries Resilience4j will attempt on failure
The maximum number of output tokens the model is allowed to generate before being forced to stop
The size of the HTTP connection pool used to reach the provider
explanation: maxTokens caps decode-phase output length, directly bounding the most expensive and highest-latency part of a request; leaving it unset risks unbounded cost and latency from a rambling generation.

promptText: Using Little's Law (L = lambda x W), if your chat endpoint has an average end-to-end latency of 3 seconds and you expect 20 requests per second at peak, how many concurrent in-flight requests must your system sustain?
explanation: L = lambda x W = 20 x 3 = 60. Your thread pools, HTTP connection pool, and the provider's own rate limit must all be able to sustain 60 concurrent in-flight requests.

promptText: A team reorders their prompt so a per-request timestamp and reordered few-shot examples appear before the large static system prompt. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Latency improves because the model processes recent information first
Provider-side prefix caching is defeated because the prefix is no longer byte-identical and consistently positioned across calls
The embedding model will refuse to process the request
Cost is unaffected since only output tokens are billed differently
explanation: Prefix caching requires the static content to appear first and be byte-identical across calls; inserting dynamic content before it breaks the prefix match, so every call pays full price and full prefill latency.

promptText: Why is reporting average latency instead of p95/p99 considered a common mistake?
options: Averages are mathematically incorrect for latency data
p95/p99 are always lower than the average, making the system look better
A system can have a great average while a meaningful fraction of requests suffer high tail latency, and averages hide exactly the failures that drive user complaints
Percentile metrics are required by most cloud providers for billing purposes
explanation: Averages can look healthy even when a system has a bad tail; percentile latencies (p95/p99) surface the outlier behavior that actually causes user-visible pain, which averages mask.

promptText: What is the key difference between adopting Java virtual threads and migrating to WebFlux to handle blocking model calls at scale?
options: Virtual threads require rewriting all Advisor and business logic in a reactive style, while WebFlux does not
Virtual threads let you keep the simple synchronous programming model while avoiding thread exhaustion under blocking I/O, whereas WebFlux requires an event-loop, non-blocking rewrite
WebFlux is only usable with Spring MVC, not Spring AI
Virtual threads eliminate model provider latency entirely, while WebFlux does not
explanation: Virtual threads solve platform-thread exhaustion from blocking I/O without changing the synchronous programming model; WebFlux solves the same class of scalability problem but requires adopting reactive, non-blocking composition throughout.

promptText: Users start seeing chat answers meant for other users after a response cache is added. What is the most likely root cause and fix?
options: The cache TTL is too short and should be increased
The cache key omits an identity/context dimension (like user or tenant ID); the fix is to include every input that affects correctness in the cache key
The embedding model was changed without re-indexing
Streaming was enabled without a circuit breaker
explanation: Caching purely on message text without including user, tenant, or conversation identity produces cross-contaminated answers; cache keys must include every input that affects the correct answer, not just the most visible text.

promptText: Why does a tool-calling (function-calling) interaction typically cost more latency than a plain single-turn chat completion?
options: Tool calls always use a larger, slower model
It requires multiple sequential prefill/decode round trips: the model generates a tool-call, the tool executes, and the result is re-processed as new input before a final decode pass
Tool calls disable streaming entirely
Tool calls are billed at a flat rate regardless of round trips, so latency is unaffected
explanation: A tool-calling turn is not one prefill/decode pair but several: an initial decode to request the tool, a second prefill over the appended tool result, and a final decode -- each additional tool call compounds this cost.

promptText: A team scales their Spring Boot replicas from 3 to 10 to handle more traffic, but starts seeing a wall of HTTP 429 errors from the model provider instead of improved throughput. What does this reveal, combining Little's Law with the chapter's discussion of throughput ceilings?
options: Their JVM heap is too small for the additional replicas
Aggregate concurrency across all replicas has exceeded the provider's account-wide concurrent-request or tokens-per-minute ceiling, which is the true throughput limit, not their own infrastructure
Virtual threads were not enabled on the new replicas
The circuit breaker's failure-rate threshold was set too low
explanation: Provider rate limits are typically account-wide, not per-instance; Little's Law shows required concurrency scales with replicas, but adding replicas without checking the provider's ceiling simply pushes aggregate concurrency past a limit your own infrastructure cannot see or control.

promptText: A low-priority summarization feature and a high-priority chat feature share one Spring Boot application. During a summarization traffic spike, the chat feature's latency degrades too, even though it uses a different code path. What Resilience4j pattern directly addresses this, and why does it differ from a circuit breaker?
options: A Retry policy, because it adds backoff that smooths out traffic spikes for both features equally

A Bulkhead, because it isolates each feature's resource pool (threads/concurrency) so saturation in one feature cannot consume capacity needed by another -- a circuit breaker only reacts to failure rate, it does not partition resources
A TimeLimiter, because it caps how long any single call can run regardless of which feature issued it
Increasing maxTokens for the chat feature so it completes faster under load
explanation: The bulkhead pattern isolates resource pools per feature so one feature's saturation cannot starve another sharing the same application; a circuit breaker instead trips on failure/timeout rate but does nothing to prevent resource contention between healthy features.

promptText: A team implements a semantic cache using embedding similarity to reuse answers for near-duplicate queries. What is the central risk in choosing the similarity threshold, and why can't it be picked by intuition alone?
options: Too low a threshold makes the cache miss on every query, wasting engineering effort with no benefit

Too low a threshold treats semantically different questions as equivalent and confidently returns a wrong cached answer with no error signal; too high a threshold makes the cache rarely hit, undermining its purpose -- so it must be validated against a labeled set of near-duplicate and genuinely-different query pairs
The threshold only affects storage cost, not answer correctness
Cosine similarity thresholds are standardized across all embedding models, so tuning is unnecessary
explanation: Semantic cache threshold tuning is a genuine precision/recall trade-off: a threshold set too low silently serves wrong answers with no indication anything failed, while one set too high defeats the cache's purpose -- only empirical validation against labeled pairs resolves this correctly.
